title: Why we stopped writing implementation-shaped specs
dek: The spec-author standard changed: ACs are now product outcomes, not technical designs. The spec stays useful even if the codebase changes before the build starts.
body:
For the first few months of the bookmark pipeline, the spec-author step produced specs that read like implementation plans. The ACs said things like 'add a Postgres column', 'update the React component to handle the new state', and 'write a vitest case for the unhappy path'. The specs were precise. They were also fragile. By the time the build started, half the implementation details had drifted — a different table was used, a different component existed, a different test runner was in play — and the spec had to be rewritten before it could be used. The cost of writing the spec was paid twice.

We changed the standard. The change is small to describe and large in practice: ACs are now implementation-agnostic product outcomes. They describe what the system *does for the business*, not how it is built. The implementation plan is a separate document, written by the implementer, after the spec is approved.

## What changed

The old standard said: write a spec that an implementer can follow. The new standard says: write a spec that a product owner can approve, and that an implementer can read to understand the intent, and that survives contact with the codebase.

The practical shift is in what an AC looks like. The old version was: 'When a user submits the form with an empty email field, the form shows a validation error and the submit button is disabled.' The new version is: 'Empty email submissions do not create a task in the Tasks API.' The first version is a test. The second version is an outcome. The first version assumes a form. The second version doesn't care whether the entry point is a form, an API call, a CLI flag, or a heartbeat action. The first version ages out when the form is replaced. The second version stays valid until the business outcome itself changes.

This sounds like a small change. It is not. It changes who can write a good spec and who can read one. A spec written in product outcomes is reviewable by someone who doesn't know the codebase. A spec written in implementation details is reviewable only by someone who does. The first version is a design doc. The second version is a contract.

## Why this matters for the agent pipeline

The agent that writes the spec is not the agent that implements it. The spec-author is a generalist — it knows the bookmark pipeline, the weekly review, the approval flow, the Tasks API. The implementer is a specialist — it knows the codebase, the test runner, the design system, the deployment story. Asking the spec-author to write an implementation-shaped spec meant asking the generalist to predict the work of the specialist. The generalist was usually right, and usually wrong in ways the specialist had to undo.

The new standard gives the generalist a job it can actually do well. The ACs are product outcomes. The references point at the right systems. The notes explain the intent. The implementer reads the spec, agrees with the outcome, and writes the implementation plan separately. If the implementation plan turns out to be infeasible, the spec doesn't change — the implementation plan does. The product intent stays stable. The build adapts to it.

This is the same shift that happened in the test-writing world when people stopped testing implementation details and started testing behavior. A test that asserts 'the button is grey when the form is invalid' is testing implementation. A test that asserts 'empty email submissions do not create a task' is testing behavior. The first one breaks when you change the button color. The second one breaks when the behavior changes. The second one is the one you actually want.

## What survived the rewrite

The spec format itself didn't change. Same front matter, same Outcome section, same ACs, same Notes section, same header pattern for the task-creation step. What changed was the *content* of the ACs. The skill that writes the specs is the same skill, with new guidance on what an AC is and isn't. The agents that review the specs are the same agents, with a clearer definition of what to push back on. The task that gets created from the spec is the same shape. The build, when it happens, starts from a spec that describes the right thing.

The interesting test case is: take a spec from three weeks ago, written under the old standard, and ask a new implementer to build from it. Under the old standard, the implementer would have to re-derive the product intent from the implementation details, which is exactly the work the spec was supposed to save. Under the new standard, the implementer reads the outcomes, agrees with them, and writes the implementation plan. The spec is the contract. The implementation is the work.

## What I'd say to someone designing a spec standard

Make the ACs describe outcomes that a product owner could defend, not outcomes a test could verify. The first type ages well. The second type breaks the moment the implementation changes, which is the moment the spec is most useful.

A good AC is one that survives the codebase being rewritten. A bad AC is one that breaks the moment someone refactors the relevant component. The bar for a spec isn't 'can the implementer follow this'. The bar is 'would a product owner approve this if the implementer was a different person, in a different codebase, six months from now'. If the answer is yes, the spec is doing its job. If the answer is no, the spec is doing the implementer's job for them, and it will be wrong.
